Authentication flow

Source: vignettes/authentication-flow.Rmd
authentication-flow.Rmd

Overview

Signing in involves your app, the user’s browser, and a login provider such as Google or GitHub. The provider handles the password and asks for permission to share data. shinyOAuth checks the returning response before your app uses it.

OAuth grants permission to call a service’s API using a credential called an access token. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds a signed ID token that lets the app verify who signed in. If the provider also issues a refresh token, the app can obtain a new access token without another browser login.

For a working app, start with Usage. The UI wrapper and server module run the checks described here automatically.

What happens during the authentication flow?

1. The app starts a login

By default, the module starts login automatically. With auto_redirect = FALSE, a button can call auth[["request_login"]]() instead.

The app sends the browser to the provider with the requested permissions, called scopes, and the registered return address, called the redirect URI. Asking for only the permissions your app needs makes the consent request easier to assess.

2. The user signs in at the provider

The user enters credentials at the provider, then approves or declines access. The provider may remember an earlier login or permission decision, so it does not always show both prompts. Your app never needs the provider password.

3. The browser returns to the app

The provider sends a short-lived authorization code to the registered callback URL. Your server exchanges this temporary code for tokens, including the access token used for API calls.

shinyOAuth checks that the response belongs to the pending login and the browser that started it. An expired, reused or mismatched response cannot complete login. Keep cookies and session storage available, and finish in the same browser tab.

4. The server obtains and checks tokens

shinyOAuth exchanges the code for tokens using your app’s registered credentials. With OIDC, it verifies the ID token’s signature, intended recipient, expiry and connection to this login request. If a profile is also fetched, its subject must match the validated identity when both are available.

Decoding a token reveals its contents without verifying them. The signature and login checks verify the identity data before the app accepts it. OAuth-only providers such as GitHub and Spotify supply profile information through their own APIs.

5. The app uses the authenticated session

Only after the required checks pass does auth[["authenticated"]] become true. Use it in server code before reading private data or taking an authenticated action:

output[["greeting"]] <- shiny::renderText({
  shiny::req(auth[["authenticated"]])
  paste("Hello,", auth[["token"]]@userinfo[["name"]])
})

Profile fields depend on the provider. Login establishes an identity under the configured checks; your app still decides which accounts may view a report or perform an action. Hiding a button alone does not protect the server code.

Why login needs state, PKCE and a nonce

These values protect different parts of the same exchange. shinyOAuth manages them for you; follow your provider helper’s registration guidance.

Protection Purpose
State and browser binding Connect the returning response to the pending login and initiating browser.
PKCE Tie the code exchange to the app that prepared the authorization request.
OIDC nonce Tie the returned ID token to this particular login request.

Do not share complete login URLs or copy private browser inputs into logs or bookmarks. Browser binding does not decide which account you expected: check the validated identity against your own access policy when that matters.

Token expiry, refresh and signing in again

Access tokens usually expire. If the provider issues a refresh token, the module can refresh before expiry with refresh_proactively = TRUE. The app then uses the replacement token through the same module or connection.

Use reauth_after_seconds when users must sign in again after a maximum period. Refreshing an API token does not restart that timer. Keep indefinite_session at its default FALSE unless your app deliberately needs a different expiry policy. With that option enabled, local login state can outlast usable API access.

Token exchange and refresh are not automatically repeated after ordinary network failures: the provider may already have consumed the code or rotated the refresh credential. Offer a new login when access cannot be renewed.

Logout and token revocation

auth[["logout"]]() clears the app’s local login and attempts token revocation when the provider supports it. It does not sign the user out of their Google, GitHub or other provider account. A later login may therefore reuse that account.

Clear or guard private results when login changes, so a failed revocation request cannot leave the previous user’s data visible after local logout.

Additional provider and deployment requirements

Some providers need signed requests, certificate-bound tokens or a different callback format. These extend the same flow; configure them only when the provider and deployment support them. See Advanced security for the purpose and setup of each feature.

Apps using several providers need to distinguish their callbacks. Prefer the distinct registered routes shown in Multiple authorizations. If a callback can reach another R process, follow the shared-store guidance.

Diagnosing a failed step

Use audit logging to find the failed operation. Keep validation enabled while checking callback URLs, credentials and permissions.

For exact validation rules and settings, see oauth_client(), oauth_provider(), handle_callback() and refresh_token().
